This study introduces a computer program designed to symbolically calculate various properties of crystal layer groups, which describe movements within two-dimensional periodic systems. The script, written in Python and accessible via a web portal at layergroups.net, offers a user-friendly front end that interfaces with a high-efficiency C-based backend. This computational engine relies on a combination of the Trotter and Malcev algorithms to manage conjugacy classes and central extensions, respectively. Additionally, the software employs established methods by various researchers to handle orbital symmetries and split symbol generators. By automating intricate mathematical operations, the program facilitates rapid symbolic calculations that enable both researchers and students to access detailed group property data instantly through its accessible design.

This work introduces a novel family of non-trivial examples of non-linear Feynman manifolds, derived from intrinsically curved manifolds carrying operators labeled "momentum." Specifically, we define intrinsically curved operators $\mathcal{A}_\alpha$ parameterized by real numbers, which generalize both the standard intrinsically curved operator $\mathcal{A}_1$ proposed by Stara\k{r}a and the differentiation operator on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Our primary achievement is the construction of a unitary transform capable of diagonalizing every $\mathcal{A}_\alpha$ operator. This transformation is conceptualized as a fractional integration operator, valid particularly for $\alpha > 1$. The operator's domain is a dense subset consisting of smooth functions finite under specific derivative conditions. Notably, when the underlying manifold is of compact type, we demonstrate that the domain of definition for these operators encompasses the entire manifold.

Deforming the integration contours offers a method to alleviate the sign problem encountered by Monte Carlo simulations away from half-filling. However, the resulting Jacobian determinant within the Boltzmann weight can exhibit large fluctuations, hindering effective sampling. This study introduces a feedback algorithm designed to mitigate such Jacobian fluctuations, applicable to continuum quantum charge liquids. By comparing algorithm performance at various fillings, we found that while sampling improves notably, a residual sign problem persists at low densities. Furthermore, distorting contours yields significant advantages even in the half-filling limit, where a traditional determinant-weight Monte Carlo approach faces no sign problem; here, the proposed algorithm accelerates sampling, particularly deep within the incompressible sea phase.

We introduce a novel framework for the composite Higgs model, which is built on a global $SO(5)/USp(4)$ symmetry breaking pattern. In this scenario, the composite sector features a scalar singlet that couples to the Standard Model (SM) via a portal interaction with the Higgs boson. By employing an $SO(5)$-invariant effective field theory (EFT), we analyze the dynamics of the Higgs potential, radiatively generated mass for the singlet scalar, and the associated SM observables. Specifically, we examine the impacts of the singlet coupling on the trilinear self-interaction of the SM Higgs boson and its mutual $ZZ$ interaction. Finally, we assess the experimental viability of this scenario by comparing its predictions with current collider data from LHC Run 2.

Virtual-Physical Perceptual Manipulations (VPPMs) involve sending distinct patterns of virtual versus physical stimuli to users to either enhance or alter their virtual experiences. These VPPMs have been utilized in research to facilitate more refined and complex control over virtual objects within desktop VR setups by extending beyond standard 3DOF/6DOF motion platforms. Our paper introduces a unified modeling framework for VPPMs, offering detailed descriptions for implementing various manipulation types. To demonstrate the utility of this approach, we present a VR application designed for teleoperation that utilizes three specific VPPM types: vibration desynchronization, velocity desynchronization, and haptic forewarning.

We evaluate various methods for integrating new languages—specifically German and Korean—into BigScience's 1.3-billion parameter multilingual pre-trained model. This model originally supports 13 languages. The research examines how different factors influence language adaptation performance and assesses the tradeoffs between computational resources and anticipated results.

Recent research has revealed that the majority of stars form as binaries, prompting a critical need to comprehend the physical mechanisms governing fragment mass. This study employs high-resolution simulations of core collapse within the framework of gravito-turbulent fragmentation to investigate this phenomenon. We utilized an adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) simulation featuring a $1000 M_{\odot}$ parent core, which encompassed a Boné-Holmberg sphere of $10 M_{\odot}$ at its center. Our results indicate that the masses of the resulting binary companions are not governed by the thermal or turbulent Jeans lengths, nor are they independent of the collapsing parent core's mass. Instead, the mass distribution of the binary fragments is directly linked to the mass of the parent core. Furthermore, the initial rotation of the parent system significantly alters the collapse dynamics and the subsequent mass distribution of the fragments. These findings offer new insights into the physical constraints shaping the binary stellar initial mass function (IMF).

This research introduces the 'm-arcsinh' kernel combined with FastICA (designated as m-ar-K-FastICA) for independent component analysis. The core innovation lies in utilizing the inverse hyperbolic sine ('m-arcsinh') kernel to construct raw data into a feature space capable of enhancing algorithmic nonlinearity. Consequently, this kernel augmentation enables the extraction of features from random data with greater reliability and randomness. The study validates the proposed methodology through simulation analyses and a dataset comprising 300 spectral images of plant leaves infected with *Pseudomonas syringae* pv. tomato. The findings demonstrate that m-ar-K-FICA successfully isolates five distinct components, three of which exhibit strong correlation with pathogen concentration. Furthermore, when evaluating predictive models based on these components, m-ar-K-FICA surpassed conventional algorithms in accuracy, achieving an R² score of 0.9650 and an RMSE of 0.0033.

This research investigates the limitations of Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT), a logical framework capable of processing arbitrary structures through symmetric evaluation, on the specific domain of simple graphs with bounded degree. First, we demonstrate that if two non-isomorphic graphs on $n$ vertices can be distinguished via CPT, then a non-tautological formula within the bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus (specifically excluding taologies over $\mathbb{R}$ or using a bounded number of variables relative to $n$) exists regarding those same graphs. Consequently, the ability to distinguish any pair of non-isomorphic graphs using CPT serves as an upper bound for polynomial-time reasoning in this specific extended polynomial calculus framework. Second, we establish that certain tautologies inherent to transitive graphs admit distinctions in CPT; this finding establishes a specific lower bound for the bounded-degree extended polynomial calculus, indicating that certain statements cannot be proven false within that system.

The concept of a cover, first developed by A. Melvin and subsequently generalized by D. K. Harrison, is introduced here for unital associative algebras. In Harrison's framework, the covering number—the smallest cardinality of a cover—was examined for specific associative rings. In contrast to ring systems, which typically feature only a singular cover consisting of invertible elements plus one extra element (resulting in a covering number of one), noncommutative systems without an identity can possess numerous distinct covers per element. The authors explore how the count of these covers, as well as their individual sizes, vary based on an element's nature. An element is termed "uncoverable" if every component of every possible cover is a non-unit non-identity element; the text establishes that in commutative systems, all elements either remain invertible within every cover or are unable to be covered if they are neither an identity nor an unit.

Social media generates content at an unparalleled rate, creating a pressing need to quickly identify and address misinformation. However, fact-checking this content presents a significant challenge due to the absence of comprehensive, real-world datasets that accurately reflect the scale and complexity of user-generated information. To address this data limitation, our work introduces a new dataset comprising over 100,000 tweets that have been explicitly annotated with expert fact-checker labels. We also propose TFC-BERT, a sophisticated model designed for efficient fact-checking. TFC-BERT combines the tweet's text with the metadata provided by professional checkers to achieve an accuracy of 90.11%, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results by 4.64 percentage points. Furthermore, through extensive analysis, we uncover the specific difficulties inherent in tweet fact-checking and offer novel insights into optimizing performance by leveraging metadata more effectively.

Stream data, such as Twitter feeds, often signals emerging events like natural disasters, political upheavals, or public health crises. While previous research has addressed in-stream event detection using statistical or machine learning methods, this paper introduces a new approach leveraging document-level learning. By applying an adaptation of the ClustStream algorithm, we extract context streams—combinations of this paper defines contexts as specific event types—directly from the streams. Each extracted combination is then modeled using a Binary Gaussian Field to identify event instances. Our method, named BGSED (Binary Gaussian Field based Stream event detection), operates under the assumption that certain words serve as event-specific markers. We validate BGSED's efficacy through experiments on both synthetic datasets and the in-stream event detection challenge hosted by NLPSEC 2016, demonstrating that it outperforms established baseline methods.

We introduce a novel approach for estimating and constraining cosmological parameters by utilizing the skew-spectrum of the matter distribution up to third-order perturbation theory. This formulation offers a highly efficient and computationally inexpensive statistic capable of accessing non-Gaussian information. Determined via a Legendre expansion of the skewness derived from the convergence power spectrum, the method remains robust against systematics arising from finite volume and incomplete mode sampling. We demonstrate that using this weighted skewness as an additional statistic significantly enhances the statistical power of two-point correlation functions when investigating parameters like $\Omega_{\rm m}$ and $\sigma_8$. Furthermore, the statistic serves as an effective probe for distinguishing between the $\Lambda$CDM model and alternatives involving modified gravity or dark energy dynamics.

By viewing adversarial training as a game between a defender and an adversary, we introduce a variational learning approach to compute Bayes-optimal strategies for BNNs. Although this method offers a principled framework for uncertainty-aware adversarial training, solving the resulting optimization problem exactly is computationally prohibitive. Consequently, we propose a practical approximation by reformulating it as a generative flow matching problem that can be solved via simulation. Empirical results demonstrate compelling evidence supporting this approach: (1) it successfully learns robust BNNs, and (2) it leverages neural network uncertainty to create an efficient adversarial attack method.

This study examines the mechanisms driving the rapid dissemination of online rumors during the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing specifically on the "Guangzhou Dog Meat Incident" that gained traction on Sina Weibo. Utilizing established network models, the paper examines both the global properties of the rumor's propagation subgraph and its localized characteristics within individual user networks. The research focuses on two key variables: the connectivity of users spreading the rumor and the count of their influential figures with high propagation power.

This paper introduces a novel methodology for classifying hyperspectral images through dimensionality reduction and pixel-wise classification. The approach leverages the assumption that certain pixels within the spectral cubes share similar categorical traits and thus exhibit correlated spectral signatures. Consequently, the study evaluates various dimensionality reduction techniques, specifically comparing their efficacy in retaining relevant information for subsequent pixel classification. The research investigates critical parameters, such as the target dimension size of the reduced data and the compression ratio, to determine optimal configurations for accuracy. The study's primary conclusion indicates that compression rates exceeding 90% result in significant declines in classification accuracy. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate there is no universally reduced dimension size that ensures peak accuracy; rather, the best outcome is achieved by combining a specific reduced dimension size with the application of an appropriate classifier directly on that data.

The principle of sparsity underpins numerous machine learning scenarios, yet its application within trained artificial neural networks has been underexplored. Guided by the "winners-take-all" phenomenon in evolution and the recent introduction of the "sparse trained pruned recurrent computational unit" (SPARC), we introduce a novel hypothesis: that in a trained feedforward neural network, a significantly smaller subset of the units can be pruned while maintaining the network's performance at or above the original level. We validate this "sparsity hypothesis" using the newly developed unit pruning framework on a variety of standard benchmarks, including recurrent and convolutional networks for tasks such as character-level one-hot classification, image recognition, and language modeling. Our analysis further reveals a strong correlation between the degree of pruning achievable and the magnitude of overfitting observed in the original, unpruned network.

This study introduces "ProteinCS," a user-friendly Python software tool designed to calculate the $^{1}$H amide proton chemical shifts for peptide sequences. As the amide proton is typically the only NMR-visible atom in protein backbone structures, its chemical shift serves as a sensitive indicator of the local microenvironment and acts as a powerful probe for investigating protein folding and misfolding mechanisms in both experimental and computational settings. Currently, ten existing methods for predicting amide proton shifts are available; however, evaluating them often requires access to specific databases containing experimental values corresponding to identical sequences. To overcome this limitation, "ProteinCS" enables users to readily generate theoretical predictions for any custom peptide or protein sequence, thereby facilitating broader applications in research that rely on comparing these predictions against experimental data to determine the conformational states of misfolded proteins.

The loss function is central to the supervised classification training of deep neural networks. Although cross-entropy is the standard choice due to its empirical efficacy, there is currently no theoretical or practical rationale for why it outperforms others. This study investigates the influence of various losses on classification efficacy through experiments on multiple neural network architectures and datasets. Our findings suggest that architectural and contextual factors may dictate the superiority of specific losses over others. Specifically, we observe that while cross-entropy often works best with CNNs for image tasks, it does not universally dominate; for instance, generalized distance losses like squared error perform superior to entropy-based metrics with certain non-convex or implicitly defined losses. We also note that the relative efficacy of these losses can vary significantly depending on the specific dataset. To address these nuances, we propose a novel selection strategy that evaluates the performance of different losses relative to baseline metrics like accuracy and the F1-score.

Investigating correlated electron systems demands handling intricate collective behaviors that arise from numerous interacting particles. While perturbation theory fails for strong interactions, an exact solution remains elusive, so physical insights are typically extracted by reorganizing infinite series of diagrams. This work focuses on such a summation technique known as parquet theory, which concurrently satisfies various two-particle correlation constraints. We present a newly developed numerical method featuring enhanced computational efficiency for solving the parquet equations of general systems. This approach utilizes flow-based discretization combined with density-matrix truncation to freely adapt grid resolution and basis set size, significantly minimizing both memory usage and runtime. Specifically, compared to existing methods, our algorithm accelerates the calculation of diagrams lacking internal discontinuities by a factor of ten and achieves a similar tenfold speedup for those with one such discontinuity.

Recent theoretical work has suggested that the pressure-induced semimetal-to-excitonic insulator transition in twisted bilayer graphene could arise from electron-hole pairing across layers. This study employs Density Functional Theory (DFT) and DFT+U calculations to examine how interlayer coupling and correlation effects influence the electronic structure of the system. We identify a competitive relationship between these two factors, demonstrating that including interlayer coupling within a DFT+U framework restores electronic instability found in pure DFT simulations. Furthermore, we analyze the nature of the predicted gap gap by evaluating single-particle excitations and the spectral function, examining them through the lenses of both conventional and excitonic gap definitions.

Although recent advancements in Natural Language Processing have made processing free text for emotional support relatively easy, integrating these tools into real-world, resource-constrained safety systems remains challenging. This difficulty stems from the high volume of incoming messages, the limited staffing available to handle them, and the fact that these platforms often lack the infrastructure necessary to run complex processing models. To address these specific hurdles, this paper introduces a novel, cost-effective approach combining a BERT-based model with a custom, lightweight method designed to categorize the intensity of users' emotions. By measuring how strongly a message conveys emotion, the system enables operators to automatically generate tailored, human-like replies that significantly boost response rates. Testing with data from a real-world community safety platform demonstrated that this two-stage framework successfully reduces emotional messages and improves the effectiveness of operator interventions.

This study reports on the detection of a spin-triplet superconducting state in electron-doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$, which serves as a prototypical three-dimensional topological insulator. Using muon-spin-rotation/muon-spin-resonance techniques to monitor the internal magnetic field environment of implanted muons, we identified clear evidence for coexisting Cooper pair states. Specifically, we observed a Pauli paramagnetic limiting field of approximately 0.35 T alongside a superconducting transition temperature of 0.32 K. These findings highlight an unusually large suppression of the critical temperature alongside a significantly reduced upper superconducting limit in this system. We propose that these anomalies stem from the competition between the superconducting pairing and topological protection mechanisms within the Bi$_2$Se$_3$ electronic structure.

Active learning (AL) aims to build an effective classifier using minimal labeled data by intelligently choosing highly informative unlabeled samples to prioritize for annotation. While most existing AL approaches rely on either querying the highest probability of being misclassified by current models or selecting data furthest in feature space, these methods often struggle with certain challenging applications. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel mixed strategy that combines both probability and distance criteria to determine sample selection. We evaluate the proposed method across three datasets for image classification tasks—two of which involve highly confounding class boundaries—and demonstrate a significant improvement in performance over current state-of-the-art techniques when labeled data is scarce.

This study introduces a novel metric known as loudness complexity to evaluate the dynamic range of music. By analyzing over 100,000 songs from the Million Song Dataset, the research demonstrates that this metric offers music genre classification capabilities that are as effective as traditional acoustic features. Furthermore, the metric has predictive utility for release year, achieving over 80% accuracy; while it only forecasts song tempo with slightly lower accuracy (around 65%), it reveals a significant trend in musical production: average loudness complexity has risen more than 100% from the 1960s to the 2000s, and average tempo has increased by 65%.

We examine a stochastic process beginning with one number in a block. At each step, a new number either extends an existing block by joining it with its current number chosen with probability $p(x)$ or initiates a new block of length $x \ge 1$. Under the assumption that $p(x)$ is non-increasing, we establish a zero-one law for finitely infinite events. For trials with finite events we obtain precise results and under additional conditions on $p(x)$ we derive a central limit theorem for block lengths. The paper concludes with examples demonstrating various theorems applied to different $p(x)$ functions.

Peirce originally formulated the inversion principle for classical logic, but it has since been adapted for intuitionistic natural deduction. Although this doctrine is intuitively appealing and widely accepted, its logical consequences are often underexplored. This study introduces the intuitionistic version of the principle formally within the Lean proof assistant and demonstrates both its validity and utility in various aspects of proof theory. Specifically, it can serve as a foundational basis for proving the uniqueness of derivation, the metatheorems regarding logical equivalences, and even the normalization procedure itself—all concepts typically established via different methods. Furthermore, various corresponding results for derivation-by-context are explored in relation to this principle.

Human preference is an essential method for defining task objectives in artificial intelligence, yet eliciting these preferences traditionally relies on tedious, one-off annotations that are poorly suited for modeling the complex, shifting preferences of non-digital users. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a feedback interface designed to capture users' evolving preferences via their digital footprints. By leveraging a latent preference manifold, our system translates discrete digital annotation tasks into continuous preference surfaces, effectively estimating users' intentions based on broader patterns of online activity. Evaluations across three distinct datasets demonstrate that this proposed paradigm outperforms both standard approaches relying on digital footprints and those based on conventional preference learning.

This work investigates how properties of Smyth powerspaces reflect the characteristics of their underlying spaces. We demonstrate that a space is locally compact if and only its Smyth powerspace is core-compact; similarly, a topological space $X$ exhibits an exponential topology precisely when its Smyth powerspace is Hausoffard. Additionally, we prove that core-compactness of the Smyth powerspace serves as a local compactness test for the space. Finally, we show that if a topological space $X$ is both core-compact and locally sigma-compact, then its Smyth powerspace is, respectively, locally compact or a manifold.

This work investigates the behavior of ideal 2D fluid vortex loops possessing pointed singularities in the context of the Euler equation. By merging techniques from variational calculus with complex analysis, we demonstrate the existence of solutions featuring such singularities and provide an explicit calculation of the associated K\'arm\'an gamma for the case where the pointed vortex loop forms a cusp.

This paper demonstrates that the estimator proposed by Belloni et al. (2014) as part of their Doubly Robust framework—specifically utilizing ridge regression for auxiliary variable estimation—retains the fundamental attributes of its double-robust, cross-fitting-enabled, and semi-parametrically efficient predecessor. Additionally, we introduce nAIPW, an extension of the estimator suited for scenarios involving missing treatment assignments. Our analysis establishes that nAIPW maintains the same guarantees of consistency, double robustness, and efficiency as the original AIPW estimator.

Particle physics evidence suggesting a breakdown in lepton flavor universality, potentially signaling new physics beyond the Standard Model, is primarily driven by discrepancies involving tau leptons. While the Standard Model predicts a specific ratio of branching fractions for tau versus muon leptons decaying via the weak interaction into hadrons, recent experimental measurements consistently show these ratios are significantly lower than predicted. We present an analysis of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, utilizing a data sample of 300 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the CMS detector at the LHC. We examine $\tau^+ \to K^+ \nu_\tau$ and $\mu^+ \to K^+ \nu_\mu$ decays occurring alongside jets produced from $pp$ interactions. Our measurement yields branching fractions of $(4.2 \pm 0.4 \text{ (stat)} \pm 0.4 \text{ (syst)}) \times 10^{-5}$ for the tau decay and $(2.8 \pm 0.3 \text{ (stat)} \pm 0.2 \text{ (syst)}) \times 10^{-5}$ for the muonic decay. These results are in good agreement with Standard Model expectations and align well with previous findings. The relative precision of our measurement is approximately 18%, yielding a ratio of tau-to-muon branching fractions of $1.52

This study introduces a new, efficient, and parallelizable numerical model for atmospheric circulation designed to run on multicores computer architectures. We utilized the Model for a Large-scale Atmospheric General Circulation (MALAG) to conduct extensive numerical experiments, specifically examining cyclogenesis and the development of tropical cyclones. These simulations were performed on commercial hardware ranging from multicore processors containing a single Intel Xeon E5-2609 CPU to the high-performance CINECA supercomputer CINECA. We also assessed performance using the Amos benchmark to evaluate parallelization efficiency. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed numerical scheme effectively captures atmospheric dynamics and achieves optimal parallelization performance.

Modelling extreme values within the upper tail of a distribution is often threshold-dependent, meaning estimates are valid only for specific quantiles relative to a chosen threshold. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a robust, reliable approach using invariante model parameters that remain unchanged regardless of the threshold's selection. These models leverage the modeling of exceedances over a high threshold, applying the Generalized Extreme Value (GEV) distribution, which is defined by four parameters: $\mu$, $\sigma$, $\xi$, and $u$. While $\mu$ and $\sigma$ characterize the lower tail and are best estimated using methods like Method of Moments or Maximum Likelihood on data below a low threshold, the extreme tail behavior described by $\xi$ and $u$ is typically fitted using Maximum Likelihood on available data. However, this paper proposes a novel Maximum Likelihood estimation technique for the tail-specific parameters $\xi$ and $u$, applicable to multiple (even ultra-conservative) thresholds. By leveraging these threshold-invariant estimates, researchers can significantly enhance the precision, robustness, and reliability of their extreme value analyses.

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) trains agents using a fixed dataset of state-action trajectories collected by a prior agent. Although this setting eliminates the need for real-time data gathering and online interaction with the environment, agents remain vulnerable to static data poisoning attacks by an adversary who modifies a portion of the dataset. In this paper, we investigate the robustness of offline RL systems against an adversary capable of fully rewriting policy-dependent sublinear portions of the dataset. By adopting a generative modeling framework, we establish that even with limited budget modifications, adversarial attacks can completely overwrite the distribution of an agent's actions in large dataset fractions. Consequently, the best possible policy an agent can learn degrades to the level found in highly contaminated online RL scenarios, representing a significant drop from the performance achievable in contamination-free offline offline RL. To address this vulnerability, we introduce a method that identifies and filters out corrupted data by modeling both the clean and contaminated portions of the dataset separately. Our experimental results on offline RL tasks demonstrate both the effectiveness of this approach in enhancing robustness and its sample efficiency.

This paper establishes logarithmic convexity as a consequence of an observability estimate at a critical time for 1-D hyperbolic parabolic systems. Specifically, we demonstrate this property for 1-dimensional heat equations featuring both second-order and zeroth-order zero boundary/zero dynamic boundary conditions. Our approach relies on proving a Carleman estimate applicable to coupled elliptic equations. As a direct outcome, we derive distinct non-existence and conditional non-existence criteria regarding finite-time blow-up. Furthermore, assuming a logarithmic convexity principle for blow-up non-existence, we prove a uniqueness theorem. These results extend and generalize previous research by Zhang et al. (2019) and Li et al. (2020).

Detecting whether test instances belong to the same distribution as training data is a critical challenge with far-reaching implications for safety and reliability across AI applications. This survey examines recent literature on this topic, highlighting two dominant detection strategies: density estimation, which is effective at catching missing test instances but often struggles with shift-invariant transformations, and classification confidence, strong against invariant features yet weaker regarding missing class detection. Although many proposed methods attempt to merge these approaches, the current state of the art remains divided into these two categories. Our review of 106 studies concludes that neither class of methods universally dominates; rather, each excels in specific scenarios. Consequently, there is a clear need for rigorous benchmarking to identify generally effective solutions and a driving push toward developing conceptually novel detection frameworks.

Recent breakthroughs in manipulating single molecules via the scanning tunnelling microscope (STM) have opened the door to developing molecular machines and artificial motors. These systems function by converting an electric current into mechanical movement at the molecular level. We conduct a time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) study on a prototypical artificial motor previously examined using *ab initio* methods by Landolt and co-authors. Specifically, we examine the role of charge dynamics in the redox-driven conformational changes of the molecule and apply an open quantum system approach to assess how including decoherence influences the motor's performance. Our findings indicate that charge oscillations play a minimal part in the configuration switch, while the classical limit of decoherence offers the most favourable conditions for the motor's motion. Additionally, we explore how variations in the STM tip's position affect the motor's movement and observe a similar effect when considering different redox species in the configurational dynamics of the system.

Origin semantics for transducers were introduced in 2016 as a tool for representing and manipulating ranked trees, offering capabilities classical semantics could not achieve. Despite this enhanced expressivity, origin-based transducers in certain configurations still simulate classical transducers. This paper investigates fundamental properties of transducers operating with origin semantics, focusing on single-valued functions and rational kernel constraints. We analyze decidability regarding language equivalence and reduction to a single classical transducer, demonstrating that while single-valued functions under origin semantics are fully decidable under these constraints, limitations arise for general semantics.

This paper introduces a new technique designed to compute the $f$-Convolution of two domain-sized $n$ functions with an $n^{2 - \epsilon_f}$ time complexity, where the parameter $\epsilon_f$ lies in the range of $\big[0, \frac{1}{d+1}\big]$ for any dimension $d \geq 1$. Although determining a matching lower bound remains an open challenge, our upper bound is achieved by generalizing the generalization of Brute-force methods, which are enhanced by exploiting the structure of the function $f$.

We have applied the forward-modeling software, forward, to high-resolution near-infrared spectra of the exoplanet GJ 229B. The analysis utilizes datasets from the Infrared Spectrograph (IRIS) on Keck I and the Near-Infrared Spectrograph (NIRSpec) on the VLT, both covering the 0.8 to 2.5 $\mu$m wavelength range. Our models, which incorporate molecular opacities, thermo-chemical equilibrium, non-equilibrium nitrogen chemistry, and N$_2$-dominated clouds, were run across a grid of atmospheric parameters. The model selection process relied on reduced chi-squared statistics ($\chi^2_{\nu}$) and visual inspection of generated spectra. Our preferred outcomes indicate an atmospheric mass of 15 M$_{\mathrm{Jup}}$ and an effective temperature of 550 K. These specific results yield a best-fit effective temperature of 500 K and an atmospheric mass of 14 M$_{\mathrm{Jup}}$, which align with prior findings. However, our analysis also reveals a notable discrepancy regarding the abundance of N$_2$; our model predicts a density of 1.0, whereas the observed data suggests a value of 0.5. This discrepancy cannot be resolved by adjusting the atmospheric metallicity. Our findings suggest that the issue may stem from an incomplete understanding of N$_2$-dominated cloud microphysics

To investigate potential exotic configurations, we performed global fits of QCD convolution sum rules, specifically targeting the $J^{PC}=0^{-+}$ hybrid meson hybrid below 2 GeV. This analysis involved four channel-specific sum rule equations to discern a putative hybrid meson state with quantum numbers $0^{-+}$ below the 2 GeV threshold. By analyzing the channel symmetry of these sum rules, we assessed the feasibility of hybrid mesons. Our results indicate significant inconsistencies across the different channels, leading us to conclude that no state below 2 GeV exhibits the quantum numbers $0^{-+}$ hybrid meson.

This document presents an updated analysis of the time-dependent decay rate of $B^0 \to J/\psi K_S^0$, utilizing $B\bar B$ events from $e^+ e^-$ collisions at the $\psi(4S)$ resonance. The data, comprising $590~\mathrm{nb}^{-1}$ collected by the Belle detector at the KEKB asymmetric-energy $e^+ e^-$ collider, exhibits a significantly enhanced $B$-meson production cross-section compared to prior datasets. This improvement enhances both the statistical precision of the measured mixing-induced CP-violating phase, $\phi_M$, and the decay phase, $\phi_D$, along with better constraints on the relative CP-violation phase difference, $\delta$.

Airborne viruses are carried within minute droplets suspended in air, a behavior driven by natural buoyancy or forced air currents. This study examines the transport of virus-containing aerosols in confined environments, such as hospital waiting rooms or office buildings, utilizing a stochastic advection-diffusion framework. This model accounts for coalescence, Brownian motion, turbulent dispersion, and the cooperative effects of multiple exhalers to simulate viral dispersion. We apply a Poisson-based infection criterion to determine the probability of transmission between individuals. Our findings indicate that while droplet sedimentation and Brownian motion play significant roles in viral transport, turbulent airflow exerts the most substantial influence. We further observe that, in certain scenarios, the expected count of infectious particles in the air can surpass concentrations immediately exhaled by the source. These results are presented to assist in air quality monitoring and the development of effective biological risk assessment models.

Building upon recent large-scale interacting valence-space shell-model (IVSM) structure findings for the $A=39$ to $58$ mass regions, this study examines $\beta$-decay characteristics and electron-capture (EC) half-lives across the $Z=20$ to $28$ proton sectors of the $A=54$ to $60$ isobaric multiplets. By merging IVSM structural insights with experimental measurements where attainable, we determine $ft$ values, comparative $ft$ schemes, and branching ratios for all accessible decay chains, and we forecast missing or unmeasured quantities using shell-model predictions. Additionally, we derive and discuss EC half-lives by integrating IVSM structural characteristics with experimental data on atomic wave functions. Our analysis demonstrates that IVSM calculations consistently align with experimental results with remarkable accuracy, reliably supporting the case for $2\beta$ decay modes in this nuclear domain.

Double-sided auctions, prevalent in financial markets, facilitate matching buyers and sellers, with recent research indicating their applicability extends beyond limiting transactions to a single unit. This broader scope demands more sophisticated matching algorithms, which we address by introducing double-sided ascending bid auctions featuring automatic quantity matching. Although this format has been employed by select exchanges like NYSE Arca Equities, it remains under investigation within the academic community. We rigorously evaluate the performance of matching algorithms within this auction type by simulating a wide variety of market agents. Our results reveal that, even in highly fragmented demand scenarios, auction efficiency can remain remarkably high.

We examine $F$-wave bottom mesons within the framework of heavy hadron effective field theory (HEEFT). This study involves estimating the masses of bottom mesons with spin-parity $J^P=1$ using light quarks, specifically fitting parameters related to the quark velocities of $v_q$ and $v_q^\dfty$. Following mass estimation, we calculate the decay constants for these states and compare our theoretical predictions against available lattice QMC simulations and experimental measurements.

This study investigates the dynamics of periodic configurations within the framework of a one-dimensional shift of finite type, $\sigma: Per(X) \to Per(X)$, where $X$ represents a sofic shift. We introduce a novel technique to identify all nonexpansive lines—specificals straight lines along which the Lyapunov exponent remains constant—within the metric space $(Per(X), d_{\text{Ham}})$. Consequently, these lines enable the refinement of an existing upper bound for the Lyapunov exponent when $\sigma$ is restricted to $Per(X)$.

The surging availability of data has triggered a surge in complex, adaptive systems, necessing data-driven modeling techniques to capture their inherent dynamics. This paper introduces a novel neural network architecture designed to learn multiple hypothesized dynamical systems from training datasets and rigorously quantifies the discrepancy between predicted and actual system behaviors using a rigorous metric. Specifically, the proposed framework addresses three primary challenges prevalent in current dynamical system modeling: (1) the difficulty of pre-defining system structure and associated parameters, (2) the lack of guaranteed bounds for system drift when no system exists, and (3) the absence of effective bounds for system deviation when valid systems are identified. Extensive numerical experiments validate the method's efficacy, demonstrating robust performance under varying system complexities and data conditions.

We propose a chess opening recommendation system that capitalizes on the inherent structure within opening databases. By modeling these openings as a relatedness network, we define similarity based on their frequency distribution across games played at equivalent stages. This relatedness concept extends beyond direct transitions to form a network of interconnected openings, which aids not only users by proposing strategically similar alternatives but also researchers in defining clusters for widely played sequences. Additionally, the network facilitates wide-ranging recommendations by suggesting closely linked openings even when a user's current sequence is statistically rare.

This study investigates key properties of millisecond pulsars—including magnetic field strength, spin period, and mass—and explores how these relate to one another and to pulsar formation. We begin by outlining a standard evolution model for millisecond pulsars and examine existing observational evidence. Furthermore, we propose a new single-zone accretion model for low magnetic field millisecond pulsars, demonstrating that it aligns well with observational data. By applying this model, we derive a correlation linking magnetic field strength to spin period and calculate the mass of accreting pulsars based on system geometry and dynamics. Our analysis reveals a critical geometric constraint: the separation between an accreting binary system's center of mass and its combined center of mass must remain below approximately 10 km. We also investigate the mass function of binary systems containing millisecond pulsars, offering a method to estimate pulsar masses and highlighting a potential upper mass limit near 2.0 solar masses for this population.

This study examines the impact of nonlocal conserved quantities on dissipative mechanical systems. Our primary findings demonstrate that such constants of motion guarantee the global existence of solutions and provide uniform bounds in the Lagrangian framework, though this Lagrangian bound may not directly translate to bounds in generalized coordinates. Additionally, we present examples illustrating that a dissipative system featuring a nonlocal constant of motion can exhibit arbitrary Lagrangian dissipation and behavior outside the Lagrangian bound, while also showing such systems may possess further nonlocal conserved quantities. Our examples further reveal a system with two nonlocal constants of motion that fails to have one, as well as a system with three such constants of motion despite lacking a second. These constants of motion arise from specific symmetries of both the Euler-Lagrange equations and the Lagrangian itself, with our examples and further ones showing that these symmetries can exist independently of each other. Our central theoretical tool is the E-L-E method, which offers a structured approach for identifying both E-L symmetries and associated Lagrangians.

This study introduces an alternative approach to air-doodling in VR for 3D model retrieval by utilizing hand air-doodling on a head-mounted display (HMD) as an intuitive and natural input. This method leverages the abundant spatial freedom of VR to resolve the constraints of traditional 2D screen-based air-doodling while maintaining backward compatibility with existing datasets and recognition models. By proposing novel image quality evaluation metrics and exploring various image quality enhancement techniques, the researchers developed a regression model that maps air-doodling gestures to pose estimation. This model achieves significant accuracy gains, reaching 80% on the public AirDRL dataset. Furthermore, a practical prototype has been created for 3D model retrieval, demonstrating promising real-world utility.

Tidal dissipation within exoplanets often peaks during periastron passage due to orbital eccentricity, a phenomenon that is most pronounced in systems with long orbital periods. Because insolation, planetary mass, and orbital semi-major remain constant for a given pair, variations in received stellar flux due to eccentricity are entirely driven by the planet's distance from its host star. We introduce a simplified analytical framework to model the thermodynamics and orbital evolution of planets on highly eccentric orbits. This formalism effectively captures the behaviors of "periastron runners"—planets characterized by long periods, significant eccentricities, and active tidal heating. By integrating adiabatic approximations for both the planet's interior and envelope, we derive a closed equation governing orbital decay, a result that aligns closely with numerical simulations. Furthermore, we derive an open expression describing the evolution of eccentricity, which is solved exactly to determine the limit of tidal inspiral—the orbital radius at which a planet is ultimately destroyed. Applying this theory, we examine the specific cases of HD 80606 b and HD 209458 b, calculating their respective lifetimes and end states. Additionally, our model quantifies the generation of internal heat; for periastron runners, this tidal heat flows internally, potentially driving surface geophysics and atmospheric circulation dynamics.

This study examines the relativistic gravitational collapse of a spherical fluid within an anisotropic setting, governed by the field equations developed by Leimes and Oberhettinger. Through mathematical analysis, we demonstrate that if the equation of state is arbitrary, the resulting system of partial differential equations (PDEs) remains compatible only when $f_1$ adheres to a specific PDE. Conversely, we show that explicit forms for $f_1$ enable model generation regardless of whether the equation of state is specified. Three distinct models are constructed and analyzed to explore the dynamics of anisotropic geometry; these include one model featuring a linear equation of state ($p=\omega\rho$ with $\omega=1/3$) and two with equations of state involving the parameter $\gamma$.

We establish a duality between the adjustments made to black hole extremality and energy conditions, demonstrating that modifications to the latter result in changes to the former, and vice versa. This relationship functions as an equivalence, illustrated via a feedback loop: specifying the type of current that defines an specific current condition determines the corresponding extremality correction, while that specific correction likewise dictates the current underlying the extremality adjustment. Consequently, this links various formulations of extreme charge corrections to revisions in energy conditions, and allows for the construction of new extremality rules based on them. This framework applies broadly, including to higher-derivative theories such as those with Weyl-squared terms, and remains valid in setups involving multiple charges.

Building on our previous work demonstrating that reinforcement learning can replicate the effects of endpoint-driven goal-directed motor learning, this paper investigates the underlying reasons for this success. We propose a novel network architecture designed to isolate specific components of the input layer responsible for emulating kinematic goals under endpoint constraints. Our results indicate that these identified components inherently possess characteristics similar to joint-space goals, suggesting that the reinforcement learning system's ability to successfully mimic kinematic goals does so by implicitly relying on joint-space representations. Consequently, both biological and artificial systems may achieve effective motor learning through joint-space goals simply because they are fundamentally more accessible than joint-velocity-based representations.

By introducing matrix representations for colour components, we derive a associated graded matrix algebra. We propose an algorithm that generates a valid upward planar drawing for any given directed acyclic graph, where edge lengths adhere to a specified metric and edge thickness conveys a ranked order. Specifically, this visual representation prioritizes minimal thickness, with levels of rank denoted by increasing values. Our methodology employs a family of edge weights that optimize total thickness while maintaining a planar upward layout, resulting in edges of constant, discrete widths where thicker lines indicate higher ranks. Established within this work is a metric and a corresponding algorithm capable of producing such drawings in linear time.

Image-goal navigation involves directing an agent within a simulated or real environment to a target defined by an input image. Although long-term memory mechanisms like hierarchical policies and graph search effectively enhance performance in simulated settings, they often fail in real-world environments due to excessive latency and a lack of generalization. Addressing this real-time performance challenge in actual navigation tasks is a critical yet under-researched problem. We introduce MemoNav, a two-stage framework designed to mitigate this issue by enhancing immediate performance. The first stage trains a graph-based short-term memory module to capture the spatial layout of novel environments from visual inputs, enabling efficient re-localization and path planning in the newly learned layout. In the second stage, this short-term system is integrated with a pre-existing long-term memory module to enable smooth navigation. We evaluate MemoNav across two major real-image-goal navigation benchmarks: a simulated real navigation task and a domestic navigation task. Experimental results demonstrate that MemoNav significantly surpasses state-of-the-art methods in real-time performance, successfully adapting to unseen domestic environments and achieving the highest possible score in the first experimental domain.

As the demand for wireless connectivity grows, traditional cellular networks struggle to provide sufficient licensed spectrum, creating a critical challenge for supporting emerging applications like remote surgery, autonomous driving, and real-time remote education. To address this, researchers have increasingly focused on unlicensed bands, specifically the 5 GHz ISM range, which offers a promising alternative. This study presents a comprehensive survey of machine learning techniques applied to unlicensed spectrum access, covering both medium access control and power management. We begin by examining the shared nature of ism channels and their potential for supporting diverse use cases, followed by a detailed review of machine learning models for media access control and power control. Furthermore, we identify open research issues and promising directions for future investigation within this field. Ultimately, this survey aims to provide a thorough overview of current advancements and highlight critical gaps in the literature regarding spectrum sharing in unlicensed bands.

This study introduces a new framework for addressing the collective synchronization problem in global interactions among dynamical systems modeled by a general hypergraph. We provide a graph-theory-inspired graph model to represent both the individual subsystems and their varying-order interaction hyperedges. By applying average-conservation-based coupling at a selected set of global states, we analyze how system dimension and interaction characteristics influence synchronization. Specifically, we examine system dimension thresholds and relevant constants within the average-conservation coupling function that ensure the convergence of combined trajectories to synchronization manifolds, offering concrete applications in synchronization control.

We examine operator growth in systems featuring Lie symmetry. In the associated Lie algebra representation, an initial low-entanglement operator evolves into a low-entanglement operator, maintaining its characteristics over extended periods. Furthermore, the out-of-time-order correlator (OTOC) exhibits persistent plateaus, demonstrating slow operator growth. Both phenomena are directly linked to compact orbits within group co

The structure of the Hoyle state has been a subject of inquiry for several decades, with a linear chain model suggested by early theoretical work. Recently, measurements of the direct decay ratio into alpha-particles provided significant data to address this question. In this study, we conduct a theoretical analysis using $\alpha$-condensate models to explain the significance of these experimental results. Our findings indicate that condensate models offer a suitable description of the observed direct decay ratio, aligning with experimental data more effectively than alternative descriptions based on $\alpha$-particle clustering. Furthermore, we explore various characteristics of the Hoyle state within the $\alpha$-condensate framework, including its binding energy, electromagnetic form factors, and radii, with specific attention to how these properties vary in response to changes in the $\alpha$-particle interaction strength.

Extensive experimental evidence indicates that long cracks in 2D brittle materials, propagating rapidly at a high velocity, frequently exhibit oscillatory behavior. While numerical simulations and experimental data suggest these oscillations stem from mechanical anisotropy, a definitive analytical explanation has been lacking. This study addresses that gap by deriving a key formula for dynamic fracture toughness, $K_{\rm II}(v)$, which depends on propagation speed. By incorporating this velocity-dependent toughness alongside conservation laws for energy and momentum, the work predicts both the onset and wavelength of crack oscillations. The resulting model aligns well with numerical simulations and experimental observations. Ultimately, the proposed mechanism attributes these oscillations to a hydrodynamic-like instability, where the $K_{\rm II}(v)$ relationship governs how energy conservation couples with propagational causality.

This paper establishes the equivalence between the information theoretic feedback capacity and the largest asymptotic rate of solvable games occurring in two-player interaction scenarios involving finite state channels. Additionally, we offer a novel approach to addressing infinite-horizon games with partial observations by representing the value function as the unique fixed point of a policy-dependent contraction mapping defined on the space of bounded real-valued functions over game states. Leveraging this technique, we offer a fresh perspective on demonstrating the existence and uniqueness of the game value for such scenarios.

The rise of tabular data in content like news articles, videos, and images has led to claims involving visual elements within those tables. However, verifying such visually grounded assertions is difficult because existing fact-checking tools do not handle images well and no specialized fact validators exist specifically for tables. To address this gap, the authors introduce FCT4TD, a new benchmark for fact-checking tabletop data that includes over 1,000 complex claims drawn from more than 300 complex tables. This benchmark is constructed by extracting and fine-tuning large language models to extract supporting or refuting evidence from various sources, then evaluates three progressive tasks: extracting entities and relationships from tables, identifying conflicting claims, and identifying claims supported or refuted by the input evidence, and finally, detecting tables and visually grounded assertions. This investigation explores the essential role of complex numbers in Quantum Mechanics. We survey prominent rationales commonly cited in literature advocating for complex formalism while introducing additional persuasive arguments. This concise study seeks to reinforce the challenging task of clarifying the fundamental need for complex numbers in the framework of Quantum Mechanics.

Let $G=(V,E)$ be a connected, simple, and undirected graph, and suppose $S \subseteq V$ constitutes a resolving set. This means that for every vertex $v$ outside of $S$, the vector of distances $\{d(u, v) : u \in S\}$ forms a unique signature specific to $v$. The metric dimension of a graph $G$, denoted as $\text{dim}(G)$, represents the cardinality of a resolving set with minimum possible size. In this study, we investigate graphs exhibiting symmetry under the action of a finite group, where $G$ is equipped with a faithful action $\Gamma$ operating faithfully on both the vertex set and edge set. We establish an upper limit on $\text{dim}(G)$ by analyzing the or-bits of this action and, more specifically, by selecting $G$-orbits as our resolving sets. Additionally, we examine various scenarios in which an orbit serves as an optimal resolving set.

This paper introduces a novel numerical approach designed to simulate the transport of pollutants in the saturated groundwater. The model operates across two spatial dimensions and handles scenarios ranging from near-field to infinite spatial scales. It is built upon the governing equation derived from Darcy's Law, which describes groundwater movement. The proposed numerical framework employs a numerical analog of the analytical piecewise linear solution for a differential equation, applied within a structured grid. This solution accounts for pressure gradients, the pollution source term, and Darcy's coefficient. Advection is managed using a near-field component based on an Adams-Buforv scheme and a numerical representation at large distances based on Jankov's research. For the numerical treatment of the source term, a piecewise linear solution is utilized over each grid cell. For temporal integration, an implicit Euler method is implemented. The study includes a numerical analysis of the proposed algorithm along with a comparison against established results to demonstrate its accuracy.

This study introduces a novel approach to modeling the oxidation of gaseous pollutants within water treatment systems using a generalized chemical kinetic framework. Designed for integration with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) codes, this reduced order model offers significant efficiency gains over traditional methods. The reduced order scheme accounts for the fast equilibrium characteristics of key chemical reactions and demonstrates application in an electrochemical reactor utilizing ozone and ultraviolet light for gas oxidation.

This paper introduces an optimized multicore simulation framework designed for large-scale neuromorphic computing systems. By leveraging inherent similarities in memory access patterns across independent neuron simulations, our approach effectively utilizes independent threads to execute neuron computations. Furthermore, we employ the OpenMP shared memory model to minimize inter-thread communication and maximize the use of shared system resources. Testing on a cluster equipped with dual Intel Xeon processors, each featuring 12 cores and 48 GB of RAM, and running the Multi-Scale Neural Network simulator, we achieved significant performance gains. Our results demonstrate that this multicore implementation delivers a speedup of 120x to 130 times compared to the prior single-threaded single-node version.

The application of Machine Learning in safety-critical domains necessitates models that explicitly represent uncertainty. Although probabilistic alternatives like Neural Networks have been addressed, classical Decision Trees remain uncertain regarding their internal handling of randomness. This study investigates the integration of Monte Carlo Dropout into Decision Trees by proposing Indecision Trees. Evaluating both classic Dropout and Indecision Trees against a baseline using the C4.5 algorithm on a binary classification task with a noisy dataset revealed superior results for Indecision Trees. Specifically, they outperformed standard Dropout in accuracy while generating more reliable uncertainty estimates. Furthermore, they detected higher levels of noise than Indecision Trees did.

Time series analysis is a critical area within data mining that frequently relies on Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to measure the similarity between sequences. Although the $k$-nearest neighbor (KNN) classification method utilizing these DTW distances has proven effective for clustering time series, this process often suffers from both high computational costs and low accuracy. To address these limitations, we introduce EAPrunedDTW, an algorithm that simultaneously enhances the speed and precision of classification by comparing two time series. This approach functions by progressively calculating distances between DTW pruning zones; if these gaps exceed a defined threshold, the algorithm prematurely stops the computation. We evaluated our method against standard KNN using various distance metrics on two large-scale real-world datasets. The results demonstrate that EAPrunedDTW not only achieves greater classification accuracy but also delivers substantial improvements in computational efficiency compared to existing solutions.

This paper details the testing education strategy employed by the IST Student Chapter at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands. The chapter collaborates with professors to deliver a self-contained, inquiry-based learning module designed to supplement or replace formal testing courses. This module caters specifically to computer science undergraduates, offering them hands-on experience with testing principles through a self-directed study of peer-reviewed empirical research. By analyzing existing literature and constructing testing systems to validate their hypotheses regarding testing, students gain a practical understanding of testing from an empirical research standpoint. We analyzed participant feedback from two iterations of this module and compared their professional habits pre- and post-participation. The comparative results indicate that by the conclusion of the session, students had adopted industry-standard testing practices. Furthermore, survey data revealed that students found the teaching methodology engaging and effective. We conclude that inquiry-based learning is a valuable approach for equipping students with professional-grade testing practices.

Explainable AI has become a critical focus in machine learning applications requiring transparent decision-making, such as healthcare and security, due to its potential to enhance model reliability, transparency, and provide valuable insights into model performance. This study introduces a unified framework that offers a comprehensive survey of current methodologies for visualizing black-box models. By assessing these approaches against essential criteria—including usability, insightfulness, explainability, and scalability—this survey identifies a range of black-box visualization techniques and delivers a forward-looking perspective on emerging directions in black-box modeling.

Over-smoothing represents a critical challenge limiting both performance and effectiveness in Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs). Existing literature primarily addresses this by modifying the graph normalization technique, often neglecting the actual graph message passing mechanism. In this work, we examine over-smoothing from a novel standpoint and introduce the Dual-Attention Graph Convolutional Network (DA-GCN). This architecture overcomes over-smoothing by simultaneously capturing local and global contextual information. Specifically, DA-GCN integrates a Dual-Attention module that functions within the message passing layer to overlay global attention on top of local message passing. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets for node classification demonstrate that DA-GCN consistently surpasses current state-of-the-art performance in the competitive ArXiv2008 GCN challenge.

This study investigates the phenomenology of two-lepton dark matter interactions at a Z-factory operating at the FCC-ee, focusing on the $e^+e^-\rightarrow \gamma\chi\bar{\chi}$ production mechanism where final-state Z boson decays into either $\tau^+\tau^-$ or $\mu^+\mu^-$. By utilizing integrated luminosities of 1.5 ab$^{-1}$, 10 ab$^{-1}$, and 36 ab$^{-1}$ across energy stages 1, 2, and 3, we project the two-lepton reach. Additionally, by incorporating constraints from existing LEP and FCC-ee Z-pole data regarding invisible Z width, we derive the combined exclusion limits applicable at the FCC-ee.

We introduce a set of $k_\perp$-dependent functions, denoted as $\tilde{\Delta} q^{(n)}$, which encode the correlation between transverse spin vectors of participating quarks and the intrinsic transverse momentum of a hadlet carrying finite momentum, based on n light quarks. These functions find their physical motivation in processes involving hadrons with spins, specifically those with non-zero spin, and are particularly relevant for hadrons with finite momentum.

Compact support coincidence occurs within a Tychonoff cube when the topology on the group of compactly supported homeomorphisms aligns with both the compact-open topology and the topology of uniform convergence. This paper provides a characterization of such cases and demonstrates that the property fails to exist on any complete, metrizable space lacking the structure of a countable product of closed intervals. Additionally, specific examples are offered: the compact support coincidence topology on homeomorphism groups over open metric contractible spaces is shown to be strictly coarser than uniform convergence but strictly finer than the compact-open topology.

Graphene serves as an ideal substrate for the ultra-flat growth of Heusler materials, a trait essential for producing high-quality heterostructures capable of generating strong spin-orbit couplings and magnetic proximity effects. However, understanding the precise growth mechanisms remains critical for leveraging these materials in advanced device applications. In this study, we investigate the remote epitaxy of Co$_2$MnSi heusler layers on graphene, which itself grows epitaxially atop SiC. Angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy reveals that the Co$_2$MnSi lattice adopts the same orientation as the SiC template, yet thickness-dependent shifts in the photoemission spectra and the emergence of new atomic columns in high-resolution scanning transmission electron microscopy images indicate that the material does not grow directly on the graphene monolayer. These findings support a model in which the initial growth layer adopts the SiC lattice orientation, subsequently undergoing a lattice mismatch-driven reconstruction that creates novel columns. This reconstruction facilitates alignment with the SiC template for overlying co2MnSi, confirming a growth pathway characteristic of remote epitaxy. Furthermore, the presence of a distinct, atomically clean interface between the co2MnSi and the graphene suggests this method yields superior interfacial quality, a prerequisite for maximizing spin-orbit coupling and interface magnetism in these systems.

This paper demonstrates that for any specified level of non-stationarity, the set of first $m$ eigenvalues of the sample spectral density matrix among $T$ observations exhibits the same asymptotic distribution as $m$ independent identically distributed random variables drawn from the Wishart distribution with $S$ degrees of freedom and scale matrix $\Lambda_{m+1}$. This result holds under the assumption that the remaining eigenvalues of the same sample spectral density matrix are uniformly bounded. The finding offers practical insight into the estimation of $m$, which represents the degree of non-stationarity or trend in a time series, and enables the derivation of asymptotic standard errors for the estimated parameter $\hat{m}$. These asymptotic standard errors facilitate hypothesis testing with an asymptotic significance level of $\alpha=0.05$ regarding whether a specific time series dataset possesses a given estimated non-stationarity level $\hat{m}$.

We report the detection of 11 multiply lensed galaxies in the massive cluster RXC J1419.4+2202, identified through a comparison of a deep Hubble Space Telescope Wide Field Camera 3 (WFC3/IR) imaging campaign with a catalog of foreground objects. Our analysis reveals that this cluster hosts numerous high-redshift galaxies, with the new sample comprising 11 lensed systems at redshifts $z \gtrsim 2.5$ and redshifts $z \lesssim 3.5$ (with the new objects at $z \gtrsim 2.5$ and $z \lesssim 3.5$ [correction: $z \lesssim 3.5$]). This brings the total known number of galaxies lensed by the cluster to 19. The newly discovered systems exhibit significant magnification factors ($\geq 3$), which enhance their utility as probes for high-redshift astrophysics. We also characterize the cluster's dark matter halo using a $\beta$-model profile derived from the imaging data.

This paper examines a model of competition among content providers (CPs) and internet service providers (ISPs) that incorporates profit-sharing arrangements. Specifically, we investigate an equilibrium scenario in which two CPs and two symmetric ISPs compete for market share across two networks of varying quality. Under certain conditions, each ISP engages in profit-sharing with both CPs, resulting in a total of three distinct equilibrium configurations. We analyze the impacts of profit-sharing by comparing them to a non-sharing baseline where no revenues are distributed. Our findings reveal that profit-sharing allows CPs to secure higher demand and achieve greater profits. Furthermore, an ISP operates more profitably under profit-sharing unless it is completely disconnected from the CPs. Additionally, the implementation of these agreements enhances information access efficiency by the CPs and improves internet service quality for end-users.

We examine the connection between states on a C*-algebra $\mathcal{A}$ and the associated Gelfand-Naimark-Segal (GNS) representations. Specifically, we investigate conditions under which a $\mathcal{A}$-bimodule topology can be defined using these GNS Hilbert spaces. Our analysis extends to affine group actions of $\mathcal{A}$ on convex sets, covering both weakly continuous and merely measurable scenarios, as well as the formulation of $K$-theoretic index theories applicable to such indexed families.

$\alpha$-attractor models are highly relevant to observations, potentially explaining inflation through a linearly shift-symmetric potential that may arise from supersymmetry breaking. However, this symmetry often fails to hold completely, leading to curvature power spectrum deviations from standard $\alpha$-attractor predictions. We examine how potential curvature non-Gaussianity constraints apply to these modified models. Our findings indicate that for $r \gtrsim 10^{-3}$, the standard predictions are altered by orders of magnitude in non-Gaussianity, yet these alterations remain undetectable with current data but might be tested by future experiments capable of reaching $r \sim 10^{-4}$ for curvature power spectrum measurements.

We demonstrate that for any pair of measured foliations, there exists a large family of quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic 3-manifolds such that the ending laminations on the boundary components are homeomorphic to the given foliations. This finding generalizes the results found in the works of Minsky, Kim, and Kim-Lee-Kin.

This study introduces a novel statistical approach to construct risk-free investment portfolios by simultaneously eliminating both market and higher-order risks through simultaneous zero targets. The authors utilize a statistical technique to approximate the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of portfolio returns, enabling the establishment of risk-free conditions that extend beyond traditional assumptions. The study uses statistical methods to show how these portfolios can be established, alongside numerical examples that highlight the practical significance of incorporating non-Gaussian assumptions. The results demonstrate that risk-free portfolios derived under non-Gaussian assumptions offer broader applicability than those limited to Gaussian frameworks, while also providing an analytical lower bound for the minimum variance of risky portfolios. Furthermore, by simultaneously minimizing market and higher-order risks, investors can achieve more diversified outcomes, as numerical evidence indicates. The study concludes by emphasizing the potential for enhanced numerical performance through proposed statistical approximations.

Cardiac auscultation serves as a non-invasive method for identifying cardiac disease by evaluating heart sounds via a stethoscope. Although experts rely on this technique for diagnosis, its effectiveness is limited by a lack of standardization and subjective interpretation. To address these constraints, we introduce a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) designed to automatically detect murmurs from electrocardiogram (ECG) audio signals. Our methodology involves segmenting ECG audio into overlapping 500 ms windows, followed by the generation of chroma feature representations such as Bark, Log-Mel, and one-hot encodings. Subsequently, these features are processed by convolutional layers to generate max-pooling outputs, which are subsequently flattened into fully connected layers ending in a Softmax classifier. The model's parameters are refined using the Adam optimizer with binary cross-entropy loss. Evaluated on the publicly available MIT-BIH PCG database, this approach achieved an accuracy of 90.65%, a recall of 90.50%, a precision of 90.65%, and an F1-score of 90.58%.

The research into parity violation within Ce I has been expanded to encompass the $6s^2S_{1/2} - 7s~^2S_{1/2}$ electric dipole transition. Calculations involving both the one-photon and the leading two-photon partial amplitude contributions reveal that the computed matrix elements for the forbidden, spin-independent parity-violating transition align with measurements made in the $6s^2S_{1/2} - 5p~^2P_{1/2}$ line to a high degree of accuracy.

A twist is defined as a degree $4$ class residing in the topological $K$-theory of a space $X$. Interest in creating educational spaces that embrace diversity is growing. Often, discussions on this topic center remediating perceived deficits within student populations viewed as lacking standard qualities required for academic success. By contrast, our proposed framework for designing inclusive learning environments adopts an anti-deficit lens. Our approach utilizes narrative inquiry to understand various dimensions of identity and employs these narratives as catalysts for what we call "defining resistance"—the capacity to oppose dominant cultural norms. We outline six strategies for fostering community-defined resistance and provide concrete examples of their application within educational contexts.

This paper investigates the $\delta$-modulation associated with Laguerre functions. Initially, we determine the optimal range for the exponents $(p,q,\delta)$ ensuring the operator's boundedness and demonstrate its continuity across its domain. Furthermore, we derive various maximal function estimates for boundedness properties of singular integrals involving Laguerre functions and fractional integration. Finally, we analyze specific cases concerning $\delta$-modulation related to Laguerre functions and fractional operators.

This paper investigates how the perceived credibility of an auction format influences bidder strategies. By extending standard sealed-bid common value auction frameworks to incorporate an additional first-stage inquiry, we identify an auction format that serves as either a counterfeit mimicry or a credible promise. In our model, we analyze a linearly interdependent common value setting featuring two bidders who possess full information regarding interdependence parameters. Each participant must first select one of two available formats, and subsequently bids secretly in an either a first-price or second-price environment. Assuming the auctioneer possesses no initial knowledge of format selection probabilities, we demonstrate that when the platform has no advantage over another in serving as a truthful second-price guarantee, bidders may still opt to conduct a first-price auction under specific conditions.

Although descriptions of cosmic acceleration exist within General Relativity, modified teleparallel $f(Q)$ gravity theories offer an additional framework by extending standard teleparallelism through modified actions based on the non-metricity scalar $Q$. We also explore the $f_m(N)$ model's capacity to account for dark matter and dark energy as well as its potential to describe inflation. Our findings indicate an ability to replicate standard cosmological evolution while offering novel insights into current observational data regarding the universe's history.

Hessienberg varieties are algebraic submanifolds defined within the Grassmannian of a vector space, indexed by specific subsets of an ordered set of size n. Neural Painters represent a class of Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) models designed to create art in the style of specific artists.
